newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK GENERAL NEWS- JULY 11.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK GENERAL NEWS- JULY 11.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek general press:

--Greece and Turkey are looking at what their next steps will be, in the light of their agreement of principles to govern bilateral relations. Both foreign ministers yesterday stated they were working on steps that would normalise and bolster bilateral relations. Developments are expected to come to a head in September when expert committees from both countries met face-to-face for the first time and talks get under way on confidence-building measures in the Aegean.

--The government will put the issue of the agreement on the table today when the Cabinet meets. Internal ruling party PASOK dissent is also expected t be broached at the meeting, along with a joint announcement signed by 22 PASOK MPs criticising the content of the agreement and the manner in which it was achieved.

--A government-proposed candidate for managing director of the state-run railways organisation - part of the government's plan to introduce private sector managers to state-run organisations and enterprises - received the thumbs down yesterday from the parliamentary committee assigned to vet him.

--A senior forestry official yesterday resigned over the charges of state incompetence in coordinating the fight against the catastrophic fire in Thessaloniki over the weekend that effectively destroyed the city's only forest.

--Foreign Minister Theodoros Pangalos's welcome of main opposition New Democracy's stance on the recently-signed Greek-Turkish agreement prompted ND leader Costas Karamanlis to attempt to differentiate his position from the government's.

--The Greek government is awaiting Turkey's recourse to the International Court at the Hague on the issue of the Aegean islet of Imia, over which the tw NATO allies almost came to blows last year. This step by Ankara would pave the way for Greece to lift its veto on European Union funds for Turkey.

--Some 300 protestors demonstrating against the Greek Parliament's recent ratification of the Schengen treaty yesterday picketed Prime Minister Costas Simitis's residence in downtown neighbourhood of Kolonaki.

--The new radio and television watchdog body yesterday made its first strong move against a "reality show" screened on a private TV channel, imposin a fine of 100 million drachmas and requiring the channel to publicise the body's ruling at the time the show is scheduled to be screened.

--The finance ministry is preparing breaks for the average tax-payer: index-linking of the tax scale, changes in the tax-free income threshold, and reduced criteria for estimating income tax for self-employed professionals, light industry and retailers. --Maria Petrakis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
